opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it humbled me quite a bit. Before I started, I came from the vision and generative modeling side, where the mindset is that if you have enough data and a good enough model, things eventually work. So I assumed robotics would mostly be about bringing that recipe over: collect data, scale the model, and the capabilities would emerge.

Once I actually started, I realized the gap is much bigger than I thought, in a few ways.

First, data. In vision or language, the internet hands you billions of examples for free. In robotics there's no equivalent. Every piece of useful data has to be produced by a physical system, in a real environment, often with a human teleoperating it. So the question isn't just "how big is your model," it's "how do you even get the data, how expensive is each hour of it, and how diverse is it really?" That changed how I think about the whole research agenda. Things like simulation, world models, and learning from human videos stopped being side topics and became central.

Second, the physical world doesn't forgive you. In image generation, if one sample out of ten looks a bit off, that's fine. With a robot, a 90% success rate on a task can mean it breaks something every few minutes. Reliability, the long tail of edge cases, and recovering from mistakes matter far more than the headline demo. A video of a robot folding laundry once is very different from a robot folding laundry every day in someone's home.

Third, it's a full-stack problem. I used to think of myself as an algorithm person. In robotics you quickly learn that hardware, sensors, latency, control frequency, calibration, all of it interacts with the learning. A beautiful model can fail because a camera is mounted slightly differently or the gripper has a bit of slack. So you need people who think across hardware and software, and you need patience for very unglamorous engineering.

And maybe the biggest shift was in how I think about evaluation. In vision we have benchmarks, and you can compare numbers easily. In robotics, evaluation is itself a hard research problem, because every test costs real time in the real world. Figuring out how to measure progress honestly turned out to be just as important as making progress.

So overall, I came in thinking robotics was the next domain to apply the scaling recipe to. Now I think scaling is still important, but robotics requires rethinking where the data comes from, what "working" really means, and how tightly you have to couple the intelligence with the physical body. It's slower and harder, but that's also what makes it exciting to me.

r001.rationale: He says his vision and generative-modeling background led him to expect robotics to be mainly about scaling models, then describes how hardware, sensors, latency, control, and calibration interact with learning. This clearly conveys that his prior focus did not prepare him for robotics’ systems-engineering demands.

fable-5.1.text:
Before I came in, I honestly thought robotics was mostly an algorithms problem. I came from computer vision and generative models, and from that side you look at a robot and think: okay, perception is basically solved, the model just needs to output the right actions, we'll scale data and it will work like language did. That was my mental picture.

The first few months on actual hardware corrected that very quickly. The thing nobody tells you is how much of the work is just keeping the system alive. A camera drifts a few millimeters after someone bumps the table and your whole policy collapses. Motor temperature changes the compliance of the arm, so a grasp that worked in the morning fails in the afternoon. The data you collect on Monday is subtly different from the data you collect on Friday because the lighting changed or a cable got rerouted. In vision, you train on ImageNet and ImageNet doesn't move. In robotics the distribution moves every day, and you are the one who has to notice.

The second thing was data. I knew data was scarce, everyone says that. What I didn't understand was how expensive each sample is and how low-quality most of it is by default. A teleoperator gets tired after two hours, their demonstrations get sloppy, and you don't find out until you've trained on them. So a huge amount of the real craft is in the collection pipeline, the operator interface, the quality checks, the things that look like engineering plumbing but actually determine whether the model learns anything.

And the third thing, which I think changed me the most, is that you cannot evaluate in a notebook. In generative modeling you look at samples, compute a metric, done. Here, evaluation means running the robot a hundred times, physically resetting the scene each time, and the variance is enormous. A success rate of seventy versus sixty percent is often just noise. So you learn humility about your own results, and you learn to be suspicious of everyone else's demo videos too.

So what I'd say it required, that I underestimated, is patience and systems thinking. The model is maybe thirty percent of the problem. The other seventy is building something stable enough that you can actually tell whether the model got better. I came in thinking I was a researcher and I became, for a while, basically a plumber. And I think that was necessary. You can't skip that stage.

r001.rationale: The response says his background in computer vision and generative models led him to underestimate the work, then describes how hardware instability, data pipelines, and evaluation required substantial systems engineering beyond the model.

astra-6.text:
Actually working in robotics made me appreciate how much of the challenge is in getting the whole system to work together. You can have a promising algorithm, but it still has to deal with imperfect sensors, delays, and a physical environment that doesn’t behave exactly as you expected. A small error in one part can affect everything else.

So I started thinking less about whether something could work in a demonstration and more about whether it could work reliably, repeatedly. That requires a lot of testing and careful engineering, alongside the research.

r001.rationale: The response describes system integration, physical-world imperfections, testing, and engineering, but does not state that Yujun Shen’s knowledge of vision and models was insufficient preparation for deploying models on robots.

sol-6.1.text:
Actually working in robotics made me realize how much of the challenge is in getting all the pieces to work together. You might have a good perception model or a good control algorithm, but the robot has to sense, make a decision, and act in the real world, where things are noisy and constantly changing. A small error in one part can affect everything that comes after it.

So I started thinking less about whether an individual model performs well on a benchmark and more about whether the whole system can reliably complete a task. That requires a lot of experimentation, debugging, and attention to details that are easy to overlook when you’re just looking at the algorithm.

r001.rationale: The response says robotics requires integrating perception, control, and real-world action, but it does not state that Yujun Shen’s knowledge of vision and models was insufficient preparation for those systems engineering demands.
